- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is strongly bearish (≤0.00) or shows sharp negative swings, model often underestimates downside risk; add downward buffer or adjust for volatility clustering.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overcorrects and overshoots; apply a “cool-down” rule to cap forecast growth for 3–5 days.
- When true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., price drops after peak), model often fails to recognize it; use sentiment + recent price history to trigger early reversal signals.
- If model forecast is flat or trending upward with low sentiment volatility, it often fails to capture sudden downward breaks; add a “sentiment divergence” trigger to flag potential reversal.
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to overestimate early-term price stability; adjust for longer-term volatility decay or event-driven shocks (e.g., policy changes, ETS auction dates).
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model often misaligns with sentiment direction; use sentiment-weighted smoothing to reduce overfitting to recent trends.
